title: Al-Muhsi, the Counter
hookLine: the Counter, who knows every number
tomorrow: a blank page. what do Muslims say before the first word?

cards: Your phone counts your steps, your screen time, your unread messages. A weekly report shows up on Sunday whether you asked for it or not.
Grades, reps, followers, streaks: a lot of the counting in a week is done by things that want something from us. Today's Name is Al-Muhsi, the Counter.
And the Qur'an says two things about counting that seem, at first, to collide.

teach.h: HE KEEPETH COUNT OF ALL THINGS.
teach.b: The first is in Surah al-Jinn, in Pickthall's words: "He keepeth count of all things." All things. The kindness nobody saw, the shift that ran late, the tear wiped off before anyone noticed.
The second is in Surah Ibrahim: "if ye would count the bounty of Allah ye cannot reckon it." So there's the answer to yesterday's riddle.
The Counter counts everything, every deed and every moment, and the one count we can't finish is His gifts to us. He keeps the full record; our record of what we've been given always comes up short.
That changes what counting is for.
Counting can be anxious: the reps you missed, the likes that didn't come. Or it can be remembrance.

There's a hadith where the Prophet, peace be upon him, told some women among his companions to count their dhikr, their tasbih, on their fingertips, because the fingers will be asked and made to speak.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in that hadith, your fingers are witnesses. Counting on them isn't just bookkeeping. It's the body keeping a record of praise.

how: Muslims often count dhikr, such as subhanallah, alhamdulillah and allahu akbar after prayer, on their fingers or on prayer beads.

o: the Accountant who tallies only sins
the Judge who weighs deeds at the end
the Counter, who keeps count of all things

games.q: two kinds of counting — tap the pairs.
p: He keepeth count of all things
will be asked and made to speak

s: He keeps count of all things, the unseen kindness included.
the Qur'an says you couldn't count Allah's gifts if you tried
"if ye would count the bounty of Allah ye cannot reckon it."

games.q: your little cousin counts her dhikr on a phone app. her grandma says, 'use your fingers.' the cousin asks you who's right. what can you honestly tell her?
o: the app; it's more accurate, and Allah counts anyway.
the hadith gives fingers a reason: they'll be asked and made to speak.
neither; counting dhikr at all misses the point of it.
games.why: the Prophet told some companions to count on their fingertips, since fingers will be asked and made to speak. that's a reason grandma can point to; the lesson doesn't call the app wrong.

practice: Hold out one hand. For each finger, name one gift from today, small and specific: a hot shower, a message that came, a door someone held. Then the other hand.
When you run out of fingers before you run out of gifts, stop counting, and sit with the leftover.

wordCard.voice: Al-Muhsi. The Counter: nothing lost from His count, and His gifts beyond ours.

orig.note: Arabic: the Counter, from the traditional list of the Names; the Qur'an speaks of Him keeping count of all things.

carryVoice: Hold this one: counted, every good thing, by the One whose gifts you'll never finish counting. That's fifteen thirty-one.
